# Vessel Rock Lighthouse Station Notes

## Station routines

- The Vessel Rock lamp room is wound and trimmed at dusk by the principal keeper, and the lens rotation is checked against the stopwatch hung beside the door: one full turn must take 40 seconds, and if it runs more than two seconds either way the keeper writes the figure in the watch book and reports the clockwork to the district engineer in the morning. A lens that turns too fast shows a flash the pilots mistake for the Gannet light, and one that turns too slowly leaves a dark gap that has caught more than one coaster off her reckoning. The brass hand-winder is kept in the lamp room locker with its leather washers, and nobody else is ever allowed to wind the weights, because a weight let down badly will snap the cable and drop a hundredweight of lead down the stairwell.
- The fog signal at Vessel Rock sounds a blast of three seconds every 45 seconds once visibility falls below two miles, and the keeper on watch starts the engine without waiting to be told when the far headland vanishes. The compressors need twelve minutes to build pressure from cold, so the engine is warmed whenever the glass is falling fast even if the air is still clear, and the horn is tested for ten seconds each Sunday after the morning service so the village knows the trial is not a wreck signal. Every start and stop is entered in the fog book with the time, the visibility estimate and the fuel gauge, and the book is signed by the keeper who closes the signal down at the end of the weather.
- Stores come out to the rock on the relief boat, and the boat can only land at the south steps in a swell below one metre, which is judged by the keeper from the height of water on the third step. Landing a boat in a larger swell is forbidden, and the relief is simply turned back to the mainland and tried again the next tide, however short the station is of flour or paraffin. Crates are lifted by the derrick, never carried up the steps by hand, and the derrick brake is tested with an empty hook before every landing. The keepers stay clear of the landing platform while a crate is in the air, since a swinging crate has broken a keeper's leg here before.
- The paraffin store holds 600 litres in sealed drums, and the keeper checks the level every Monday with the wooden dipstick, topping up the day tank from the drums only in daylight and only with the lamp room door shut. Burning more than eleven litres in a single night is unusual and is explained in the log, because the usual cause is a cracked wick tube or a vaporiser running too hot. Spilled paraffin is mopped at once with sand from the red bucket on the landing and the sand is carried out to the sea, never swept into the drain where it would reach the cistern and taint the keepers' drinking water for a month.
- The keepers keep a rota of three on the rock and one ashore on leave, and the relief at the end of a rota takes place on the second Thursday of the month, weather permitting. A keeper coming off the rock hands the watch book to his relief in person and walks the gallery with him, naming anything that has altered since he arrived. Disputes about who has done the extra watch are settled by the principal keeper from the book, and nobody argues about them in front of the visiting inspector, whose reports are read aloud once at the Monday meal and then pinned in the store.
